title: Melbourne Beach’s water
lead: The town doesn’t make its own drinking water or treat its own sewage. The City of Melbourne sells the town its water, Brevard County treats its sewage, and the town runs its own stormwater system — the pipes that carry rain off the streets and into the Indian River Lagoon.

facts.v: “For residents of the Town of Melbourne Beach, water service is provided by the City of Melbourne Water Department.” Sewer service comes from Brevard County Utility Services, (321) 633-2091.

src.label: Town of Melbourne Beach — Water & Sewer Service

facts.v: Two: Lake Washington, part of the St. Johns River, and the Floridan Aquifer. Lake water is treated at the John A. Buckley plant (Actiflo and ozone); well water at the Joe Mullins reverse-osmosis plant. The two are blended and disinfected with chloramine.

src.label: City of Melbourne 2026 Annual Drinking Water Quality Report (2025 data)

facts.v: Permitted to make 25 million gallons a day; a typical day uses about 16 million. About 168,000 people drink it — Melbourne Beach’s 3,231 are about 2% of them.

src.label: City of Melbourne 2026 water quality report

facts.v: As of June 8, 2026 the city’s inventory counts 60,726 service lines: 41,789 not lead, 0 lead, 0 galvanized needing replacement, and 18,937 still of unknown material. The count isn’t broken out by town (Docket #8).

src.label: City of Melbourne — Lead and Copper Program

facts.v: The town runs its own stormwater utility, paid by a stormwater fee, under a 2014 master plan and a state permit. Its storm drains are marked: what enters them “flows into the lagoon.” This year’s budget gives stormwater $94,000 for repairs and upkeep and $77,078 for projects.

Two water questions. Town voters decide a $5.0 million, 20-year bond for stormwater and road projects (Resolution 2026-03). All Brevard voters decide whether to renew the Save Our Indian River Lagoon half-cent sales tax for ten years. This site gives facts on both and takes no side.

src.label: Brevard Supervisor of Elections — 2026 amendments and referenda

facts.v: From December 2020 to April 2022, 1,255 manatees died in the Indian River Lagoon event, mostly from “starvation due to lack of forage” after the seagrass died off. FWC closed the event in March 2025. Seagrass is coming back: the water management district mapped 17,042 hectares in 2025, up from 9,924 in 2023.

src.label: St. Johns River Water Management District, May 2026

facts.v: The town’s own bond page says its storm pipes are decades old, undersized, corroding or sealed off, “leaving rainwater to flow into streets, yards and ultimately into the Indian River Lagoon.” In February 2026 the commission voted up to $30,000 to remove a live manatee from a stormwater junction box.

quality.lead: The City of Melbourne’s latest report (2025 tests) lists one violation: E. coli.

rows.note: No homes over the action level.

quality.violation: E. coli was found in April and May 2025 (“an E. coli positive repeat sample following a total coliform positive routine sample”). The city ran a Level 2 assessment overseen by a third party, which found “no known issues” with the pipes or plants, and installed a dedicated sampling station. A separate August 28, 2025 boil-water notice for all customers was lifted the next day; the city said that result was likely a contaminated sample or lab error.
quality.inspection: July 24, 2026: a taste-and-odor notice after algae in Lake Washington. The city said the water “remains safe to drink” and its tests for algae toxins found none.

City of Melbourne — Update on City Water

quality.note: The report has no PFAS (“forever chemical”) results (Docket #7).

question: No town-level count was found of homes on septic tanks or of any slated for sewer. State law requires lagoon-area septic systems to connect to sewer or upgrade by 2030 (Docket #9).
